title: Why a 'Scary Stories to Tell in the Dark' Sequel Is Stuck in Legal Limbo
summary:
If you were spooked by the 2019 horror movie 'Scary Stories to Tell in the Dark,' you might be wondering when a sequel is coming. The answer? It's complicated. Director André Øvredal recently revealed that a sequel is ready to roll—but only if a messy legal situation can be sorted out.

In an interview with /Film, Øvredal explained that the rights to the film are stuck in 'copyright ownership hell.' The first movie was co-produced by CBS Films and Entertainment One (eOne). But CBS Films shut down in 2019, and eOne was sold by Hasbro in 2022 after being bought in 2019. So now, the rights are split between two companies that no longer exist in their original form. 'The rights spread out to two other companies, and then they have to agree to figure it out between them,' Øvredal said. 'It becomes about legal departments and not about creatives.'

Despite the hurdles, Øvredal is optimistic. He says there is 'movement' and that conversations happen every couple of months. 'We have a story that I love that is just ready to go whenever somebody decides, "I own the movie, let's go make it."'

The first movie was a hit, earning $104 million worldwide on a $25 million budget. It also had Oscar-winning filmmaker Guillermo del Toro as a writer and producer. A sequel was announced in 2020, but the pandemic and corporate changes stalled progress. Still, horror has remained a box-office winner, and the books by Alvin Schwartz have plenty more scary stories to adapt. So if the legal teams can untangle the mess, we might finally get that sequel.
why_it_matters: This story shows how business deals behind the scenes can stall the movies and shows you love, reminding us that creativity often depends on legal agreements few fans ever see.

perspectives.description: Fans will be excited that a sequel is already planned with a story the director loves, and the first movie was a hit, so there's clear demand. Horror remains a box-office winner, meaning a sequel could be very successful.

The tangled legal situation shows how corporate mergers can kill creative projects, leaving stories unfinished and fans disappointed. Even with a great script, years can pass without progress because of ownership disputes.

Copyright ownership disputes are a common industry pattern; when companies merge or dissolve, rights often get stuck in limbo, delaying projects for years even if artists are eager. This is a systemic problem in entertainment.

If the legal departments reach an agreement, the sequel could not only revive a beloved horror series but also adapt more of Alvin Schwartz's books, potentially launching a scary franchise for a new generation.
